Astrologers
uh-STROL-uh-jerz
n. pl.
From Greek astron, a star, and logos, word or reckoning. Webster 1828 distinguishes astrology, the pretended art of foretelling events by the stars, from astronomy, the science of the heavens. In Daniel and Isaiah the astrologers are the professional wise men of Babylon, and they are always exhibited failing.

Biblical Definition

The astrologers in Scripture are a class of Babylonian court professionals, named with the magicians, the sorcerers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers, and the narrative purpose of every appearance is the same. Nebuchadnezzar commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams (Daniel 2:2), and they could not, because he would not tell them the dream. Daniel states the conclusion for the record: The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king; But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Daniel 2:27-28). At Belshazzar’s feast the same guild is summoned to read four words on a wall and cannot (Daniel 5:7). Isaiah’s taunt over Babylon is the definitive verdict: Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee (Isaiah 47:13) — and the next verse says they shall be as stubble the fire burns. The law had already put the whole trade under the ban: there shall not be found among you an observer of times, an enchanter, a witch, or a consulter with familiar spirits.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ASTROLOGY as the pretended science of foretelling future events by the aspects and positions of the heavenly bodies, and notes that it was formerly divided into natural and judiciary — the latter being the divination Scripture forbids.

expand to see more

ASTROLOGER, n. — One who professes to foretell future events by the aspects and situation of the stars.

ASTROLOGY, n. — A pretended science which teaches to judge of the effects and influences of the stars, and to foretell future events.

Webster distinguishes natural astrology — the calculation of eclipses and tides, which is astronomy — from judiciary astrology, the divination of human affairs.

The Chaldeans were so identified with the practice that Chaldean became a synonym for astrologer in classical and later English usage.

Webster’s word pretended is the right one: the objection is not merely that the practice is forbidden but that it does not work.

Key Scripture

Daniel 2:2 — "Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king."

Daniel 2:27 — "Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king;"

Daniel 5:7 — "The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. And the king spake, and said to the wise men of Babylon, Whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."

Isaiah 47:13 — "Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee."

Jeremiah 10:2 — "Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them."

Modern Corruption

Astrology is now treated as harmless entertainment, and horoscopes appear in publications that would never print a prayer — which is exactly the condition in which a forbidden practice does its quietest work.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 18 puts divination, observing times, enchantment, witchcraft, and consulting familiar spirits in one list and calls them all an abomination, and then gives the alternative in the same passage: God will raise up a Prophet, and to Him ye shall hearken. That is the structure of the whole biblical argument. Divination is forbidden not merely because it is false but because it is a rival channel of guidance, an attempt to get the future without getting it from God. Modern astrology’s claim to be a bit of fun does not change the category; it changes only the seriousness with which the practitioner holds it, and Jeremiah’s be not dismayed at the signs of heaven is addressed precisely to people who half believed.

There is a second and more respectable form of the same instinct, and Christians fall into it constantly: the search for a technique that will yield the will of God without the ordinary means. Fleeces, impressions treated as revelation, opening the Bible at random, and the endless hunt for a personal word are the church’s own prognostication. The Reformed answer is unglamorous and sufficient. God has spoken in the Scriptures, He gives wisdom to them that ask, He governs providence entirely, and the secret things belong unto Him. Daniel’s answer to Nebuchadnezzar is the whole doctrine in a sentence: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets — and He does it when and as He pleases, to those who pray.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic ashshaph (H825), an enchanter or astrologer, in Daniel; Hebrew chabar shamayim, dividers of the heavens, in Isaiah 47:13; Greek astron plus logos for the English word.

expand to see more

Aramaic ashshaph (H825) — conjurer, enchanter, astrologer; Daniel 2:2, 2:27, 5:7, 5:11.

Hebrew hobre shamayim — dividers or observers of the heavens; the Authorized Version’s astrologers at Isaiah 47:13.

Hebrew chozim bakkokabim — stargazers, those who gaze at the stars; the parallel phrase in the same verse.

Hebrew qasam (H7080) — to practise divination; the general term forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10.

Hebrew anan (H6049) — to observe times, to practise soothsaying; the second item in the same prohibition.

Usage

"The magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans (Daniel 2:2) — the guild summoned and defeated."

"Let now the astrologers, the stargazers… stand up, and save thee (Isaiah 47:13) — the prophet’s taunt over Babylon."

"Learn not the way of the heathen (Jeremiah 10:2) — the command that covers every form of it."
